old_entry.summary: Cinema chooses where we look; a game must also account for what we decide to do. In Hideo Kojima's work, these languages meet frequently, without always seeking a comfortable resolution. Explore the relationship between staging and interaction: a pause, a voice or a gesture can change how we inhabit a sequence, rather than simply watch it.
body: Hideo Kojima (小島 秀夫, Kojima Hideo; born August 24, 1963) is a Japanese video game designer, writer, director, and producer. He is best known for the Metal Gear franchise, which remains his most famous and acclaimed work. His games are noted for being highly cinematic, the result of a passion for film and literature which began during his childhood, and he is regarded as a pioneering auteur of video games.

Born in Tokyo in 1963 and raised in Kansai, Kojima encountered cinema early through family movie nights. He wanted to draw, write and direct films; losing his father as a teenager made that ambition harder without erasing it. When he chose video games, he carried that visual education with him: editing, off-screen space and rhythm would become interactive tools.

In 1986 Kojima joined Konami as a designer and planner, when long-form storytelling in games was still considered risky. His first projects did not progress without obstacles: he had to translate cinematic ambitions into rules, memory and machine timing. The following year brought a concrete challenge, to build a war game for the MSX2. That passage connects the young would-be filmmaker to the birth of Metal Gear.

In 1987 the MSX2 could not handle many enemies and projectiles at once. Kojima reversed the problem: instead of winning by shooting, Solid Snake infiltrates, studies patrols and avoids combat. A technical limit became a grammar, turning war from a display of force into an exercise in vulnerability.

Metal Gear Solid brought stealth into PlayStation’s three-dimensional space, weaving play, voice acting, editing and real-time action together. Psycho Mantis reads the memory card and asks for the controller to be placed on the floor, making the screen feel less like a safe boundary. Kojima does not imitate cinema; he uses the console to implicate the player in Shadow Moses’s anti-nuclear story.

Metal Gear Solid 2 hides Raiden behind the promise of another Solid Snake adventure. The change of protagonist makes the player part of an experiment about expectation, control and identity. Its 2001 vision of digitally selecting facts, voices and memories anticipates a current question: who decides what deserves to survive the noise of the network?

Metal Gear Solid 3 returns to 1964 to show how Naked Snake becomes Big Boss. Survival, camouflage and the confrontation with The Boss bind the player’s body to Cold War politics. The saga no longer moves only forward: the past rewrites every familiar enemy and loyalty.

The Phantom Pain opens infiltration across large territories, day and night cycles, weather and combinable tools. Each mission becomes direction authored by the player through reconnaissance, companions, noise and improvisation. It is the series’ freest chapter and the last Metal Gear directed by Kojima before his 2015 separation from Konami.

Kojima works like a director who never forgets the controller. Actors, music, visual design, editing and game systems are treated as parts of the same direction. His photographic campaigns make that method visible: the author does more than sign the work, building a recognizable world around it and inviting cinema, fashion and music into game production.

In December 2015, after separating from Konami, Kojima established an independent studio in Tokyo. Sony immediately announced an agreement for its first project; a few months later came Ludens, the emblem of a team calling itself “those who play.” Starting again meant turning thirty years of relationships into a new creative home, one that could reach Death Stranding without surrendering an authorial identity.

Created after Kojima Productions was rebuilt, Death Stranding places connection at the centre of its rules. Sam crosses a fractured America to reconnect isolated communities; ladders, ropes and paths left by other players turn individual effort into asynchronous cooperation. Kojima uses the journey to ask what drawing closer can mean without sharing the same space. Delivering cargo becomes an act of trust toward people we may never meet.
